item.title: Healthy Mind: 6 Life Changes That Are Also Good for the Soul
item.description:
When identifying what makes for a healthy mind, we could look to any number of psychological theories for an answer. However, each theory varies in what it believes are the core components of what makes one’s mind healthy. Some theories focus on emotional awareness, while others focus more on flexibility of thinking.

Before modern psychological theories were created, the Bible spoke about how to have a healthy mind. Philippians 4:8 tells us to think about things that are honorable, just, pure, and lovely. If we aren’t used to focusing our mind on such things, it takes time to create these habits that lead to a healthier mind. Changing ways that we think and behave can be especially difficult when some of the unhealthy habits we currently possess have been with us since we were young.

Throughout our lifetime, we can learn and incorporate unhealthy habits without even being aware. Habits such as negativity, people-pleasing, distrust of others, and perfectionism (to name a few) can have an unfavorable impact on how we see ourselves, other people, and the world around us. If we continue in these unhealthy habits for long periods of time, it can take a toll on our mental health and lead to issues such as depression and anxiety.

The Nature of Creating Healthy Habits

Take a moment to think back to a time when you tried to do something new that would benefit your life. Perhaps you tried eating healthier or exercising more regularly. Maybe you decided to spend less money and to put more money away for a rainy day. Maybe you tried to be less critical in a relationship and improve communication. Were you successful in forming new ways of behaving? If so, how long did it take before the new behaviors seemed automatic?

Researchers Lally, van Jaarsveld, Potts, and Wardle conducted a study in 2009, concluding that it usually takes around sixty-six days before a new habit feels automatic. However, the time to create the new habit can vary widely (18-254 days) based on the complexity of the desired behavior, personal motivation, and the surrounding circumstances in which the person is trying to create the habit.

The good news is that the researchers also found that slipping up and missing a single day does not significantly harm the overall long-term success of creating a healthy habit (Lally et al.). In this article, we will look at six life changes that you can turn into habits that will contribute to a healthier mind as well as positively increase how you feel about yourself and others.

Remember that adopting new behaviors can be challenging, so you may want to pick one new habit to start at a time. Be kind and forgiving to yourself if you mess up because, even if you must start the new behavior again, it just reinforces to the mind that it’s worth doing.

Cultivate hope and optimism
The Cambridge English Dictionary defines optimism as “the quality of being full of hope and emphasizing the good parts of a situation, or a belief that something good will happen.” We have numerous ways of looking at the world with hopeful expectations. As a child, did you ever throw a penny into a wishing well, hoping the wish would come true? How about wishing upon a star or making a wish while blowing out birthday cake candles?

Some people believe that hope and optimism are lost once you become an adult with serious responsibilities. With this outlook, individuals can get into a habit of complaining about everything. Complaining can be contagious but hope and optimism can be contagious too. Researchers have found that both optimism and hope are related to greater happiness (Snyder, 2002; Carver & Scheier, 2014).

Optimism is often paired with hope, but they are not the same thing. Optimism is a general outlook that good rather than bad things will happen, while hope tends to be focused on something specific. Hope focused on a specific goal may make you more likely to succeed. This is what is called a self-fulfilling prophecy.

The way you think can drive your behavior to the point of success or defeat, depending on whether your thoughts are positive or negative. The cycle then begins. The more optimistic and hopeful you are, the more success you may see. This, in turn, can make a person more optimistic and hopeful in the future. The great thing about optimism and hope is that anyone can learn these skills by becoming more aware and incorporating them into their daily life.

Simple Ways to Practice Hope and Optimism

  • Look up quotes from inspiring people that foster a sense of optimism and hope. Here are some of my favorites:

“When the world says give up, hope whispers, try it one more time.” – H. Jackson Brown, Jr.

“Keep your face to the sunshine, and you cannot see the shadows.” – Helen Keller

“Whether you think you can, or you think you can’t, you’re right.” – Henry Ford

  • Every day for a week, catch yourself when you are complaining. Try to take the circumstances you are complaining about and find something positive about it.
  • Name a source of inspiration you have. It could be a person or something that provides a sense of purpose. Think about why you find them/it inspiring. Could you be someone else’s source of inspiration?

Practicing gratitude
Consider this quote from Joyce Meyer: “I’m not where I want to be, but thank God I’m not where I used to be.” This quote shows that we don’t have to have it all together to be thankful for the progress we have made.

Gratitude in our everyday lives helps us to value what we have and decrease the focus on what we don’t have. Learning to increase gratitude helps us to appreciate and savor those everyday events and experiences and can also increase satisfaction in relationships.

How do we begin to increase gratitude in our lives? Gratitude is not just something we identify at Thanksgiving or Christmas but needs to be a habit that we incorporate daily to reap the benefits. We all have things that we wish were different in our lives, but we also have numerous things for which we can be thankful.

Taking time to identify the small things that we are blessed with can help to begin a pattern of gratitude. Gratitude can also be displayed in how we appreciate others. When was the last time you thanked someone for something small that they did? Creating this habit of thanking people close to you for all the small things they do can help to develop a habit of gratitude.

Plus, you get the added benefit of having a more positive relationship with that person. Overall, gratitude is one of the easiest life changes that a person can incorporate and has the biggest social and personal payoff, contributing to a healthier mind.

Simple Ways to Practice Gratitude

  • Write a thank-you note to someone who has made a difference in your life. Explain to them what they have done and what this means to you.
  • Every day for a week, write down three things that happened during the day for which you are thankful.
  • Take a walk outside. Notice different things that you see, hear, smell, and touch. As you walk, name the things in your life for which you are grateful.

Develop an attitude of curiosity
The Cambridge English Dictionary defines Curiosity as “An eager wish or desire to acquire new information or investigate strange things.” When we think about curiosity, we might think of a child learning about the world around them or how researchers come to achieve scientific breakthroughs. However, developing an attitude of curiosity about the people that we interact with every day can help decrease conflict and develop an increased level of empathy.

We each have our own interpretations of life and how the world around us works. This is called our perspective. Our perspective is determined by many things. Our genetics, the temperament we are born with, our culture, and the experiences we have throughout life can all influence perspective.

A large part of our perspective develops during the early years of life and can be highly impacted by our early caregiving relationships. Our perspective is made up of good experiences, bad experiences, and everything in-between.

Often, we misinterpret a situation because we judge the circumstances by our own perspectives. Our brains are wired to scan for information we are familiar with that might explain what is going on in any given circumstance. The researchers at the HeartMath Institute (2019) found that we have emotional responses to our perceptions of events.

These emotional responses usually lead us to negatively judge people and situations. When we are hurt by others in those situations, we can become distrustful and feel as though we have to protect ourselves. These trust issues can spread and become part of our overall perspective of people. We put up emotional walls and begin to judge the intentions of others quickly, which leads to miscommunication and increased conflict.

It causes hurt to be continually passed on. To approach a situation without judgment takes practice and a desire to be curious about how others might view things differently than yourself. This is called “perspective taking.” This can be a challenge, since we never really know what others are thinking unless they tell us.

However, practicing perspective taking with an attitude of curiosity toward others can help cultivate a healthy mind. Having an attitude of curiosity can help decrease personal frustration, thus decreasing health-damaging cortisol levels. An attitude of curiosity can also help increase patience in yourself and strengthen your relationships.

Simple Ways to Practice Curiosity

  • Analyze the way you view others’ intentions. Are you always thinking that people are out to harm you?
  • Pick a person with whom you don’t agree on something. Try to describe the reasons why that person may think differently than you.
  • The next time you interact with someone from a different culture or geographic location than your own, ask them about their favorite thing about their culture or the place they are from.

Develop a Sense of Humor
What people find humorous can vary from person to person based on their perspective. But the fact is, people like to laugh and be entertained. After all, laughter increases social bonding and is contagious, spreading from person to person to lighten the mood. As we look around our world, we find that a lot of time, money, and effort are spent creating ways to make people laugh, such as through music, movies, and art.

There is something positive that happens in our brains when we experience humor. According to researchers at Harvard University (2010), the surprising characteristic of a joke causes parts of your brain to search for a recognizable pattern. When the punchline comes, the brain shifts from trying to process information to looking for an emotional response.

During this process, your brain releases chemicals called neurotransmitters that make you feel good. So, having a good, hearty laugh can result in positive results for the body. Laughter has been found to relieve tension, decrease pain and stress, enhance the experience of pleasure, boost the immune system, and help reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke (Harvard University). Laughter really is the best medicine.

Life can be unpredictable, not fair, and downright out of control at times. The difficulty lies in being able to laugh about a mistake we make, when a mishap occurs, or when life just isn’t rolling out how we expect. We usually can’t reverse what happens to us and, if we are alive and learning the lessons of life, we are going to make mistakes.

Humor can be a valuable way of coping when things do not go as expected. Being able to find humor in a tough situation can help lessen the negative impact that it has on your mood and decrease your stress.

Simple Ways to Practice Humor

  • The next time you are feeling down, set aside some time to watch a funny movie or watch your favorite comedian.
  • Describe a really awkward past moment in your life. Can you laugh about this today?
  • If aliens were to abduct you, describe three silly things you do that would make them send you back.
  • Next time you are struggling, exaggerate about how things might be worse. Coming up with silly ways that a situation could have gone can help you find some humor in your current circumstance.

Experience pleasure in a healthy way
Researchers have found that pleasure is an important part of healthy psychological functioning and well-being (Berridge & Kringelbach, 2015). In fact, anhedonia, which is a symptom of depression, is when a person has difficulty finding pleasure in anything they experience. You can imagine how this would cause psychological functioning to decrease.

On the other hand, some experiences of pleasure can lead to addictive behavior. Most people might agree that eating indulgent foods, winning money at a slot machine, or playing a thrilling video game can create pleasurable experiences, but too much of anything can become excessive and unhealthy.

When examining what things bring pleasure, people also find that helping a friend, solving a problem, creating something artistic, meeting a goal, appreciating nature, and engaging in calming prayer or worship also provide pleasurable experiences. Some people might even say that these latter kinds of pleasures are more valuable overall since they tend to be more lasting (Heathwood, 2013).

When pursued with a healthy balance, pleasure brings about appreciation, playfulness, sensuality, spontaneity, and a healthy focus on self-care (Huta, 2014). In fact, healthy pleasure is essential for self-care and can increase feelings of joy, comfort, and relaxation.

There is a skill used in psychology, created by Fred Bryant, called savoring that helps to enhance an appreciation for pleasure and to regulate emotional states. The skill of savoring is more than just feeling and enjoying pleasure. Savoring requires a person to put forth conscious, mindful awareness.

This allows a person to fully soak in and prolong an experience while appreciating the positive emotions they feel. Savoring can be used to experience pleasure related to things in the past, present, or future. The savoring of pleasurable experiences helps to combat negative emotions, which can lead to depression and anxiety.

Simple Ways to Practice Pleasure

  • Choose something new to try that you have never done before. Examples could be trying a new and strange type of food, engaging in a type of sport you have never tried, or researching a topic of interest that you know nothing about.
  • List at least three things you think are beautiful. Describe them and really focus on detail.
  • Name something that you used to love as a kid. Do it again, no matter how silly it may seem. If you can’t do it, then imagine what it was like when you were a kid. Remember how it made you feel.
  • Is there something pleasurable that you are doing in excess that is creating problems in your life? Create a plan about how you could use more moderation.

Create positive social interactions
Have you ever had a bad day that was completely turned around by someone just noticing you and being nice? How does it make you feel when someone walking by smiles and says, “Good morning?” Have you ever had someone pay for your order at a drive-thru? These are small behaviors that work reciprocally. This means that the receiver and the giver of the kindness both benefit.

Performing small acts, like opening the door for someone, smiling, being friendly to the person waiting on you in a store, and telling someone to have a nice day, are some of the easiest ways to change your mood. Even better, it begins to change the mood of the people around you, creating a more positive environment.

According to the Mental Health Foundation (2019), depression and anxiety are the most common mental health issues. Even though these issues are common, when we are experiencing depression or anxiety, we often think we are the only ones who feels this way. People that you interact with every day may also be feeling depressed and/or anxious. We don’t know who they are because we have all gotten good at hiding how we really feel.

Many people around us are lonely, grieving, scared, or feel forgotten. You may be feeling that way right now. Simply smiling and being kind to someone can make them feel seen, valued, and at ease.

At the same time, you can feel seen, valued, and at ease when the person reciprocates with a warm response. Incorporating positive social interactions into your everyday life can create an atmosphere of compassion and generosity, as well as help combat feelings of depression and anxiety.

Simple Ways to Practice Positive Social Interactions 

  • Do you have difficulty asking for help when you need it? How does it feel when you help someone? Find something small that you need help with and ask someone to help you. When the task is done, reflect on how it made you feel and how you think the other person felt.
  • In the morning, every day for a week, smile and say good morning to passers-by. What kind of reactions did you get? Do you think it helped increase your mood?
  • Try doing a random act of kindness for someone. Examples could be writing an encouraging message for someone in the office who may get overlooked for what they do. You could let someone with fewer groceries go in front of you in line at the store, pay for someone’s morning coffee, or when you ask someone how they are, really listen.

Where to Find Help

Some life changes are easier than others to incorporate and make into habits. When unhealthy habits become rooted in everyday life and are leading to issues such as depression, anxiety, and conflict in relationships, extra help is needed to make life changes.

Contacting our office at Texas Christian Counseling can help connect you to Christian counselors who can support and guide you in creating positive life changes that align with your values while also improving the health of your mind and the quality of your relationships.

item.title: Working Through Church Hurt: Finding Healing and Hope
item.description:
Jesus said to His disciples, “In this world you will have trouble. But take heart! I have overcome the world.” (John 16:33, NIV) Being a disciple of Jesus comes with its fair share of struggles, but the encouragement is that Jesus has triumphed over the worst this world could do to us. One particularly difficult challenge is when the source of trouble comes not from the world out there, but from God’s own people. Church hurt is a reality that many have experienced.

Church Hurt: A Painful Reality

The community of God’s people is meant to be a different sort of community. It is composed of people who are dealing with their own struggles, but this is a community being changed and transformed into the likeness of the Son (2 Corinthians 3:18), and it is a community that is led by God’s own Spirit (Galatians 5:16-26; Romans 8:5-17). It is supposed to be a place of encouragement, refuge, and growth in Christ.

All of this is what the church, the community of God’s people, is supposed to be. However, it is also true that in many ways and across many centuries, the church has also been a source of deep pain. This is true for people in the church and those outside of it. For those who can be considered insiders because they also believe in Jesus as Lord, church hurt can cause emotional and spiritual damage and leave lasting scars that require healing and restoration.

What is church hurt? Church hurt can be understood as the relational, spiritual, physical, and emotional wounds that are caused in the context of a church community. This kind of hurt can be the result of betrayals of trust, feeling excluded, abuse of authority, hypocrisy, gossip, or judgmental attitudes through the words, actions, or postures of fellow congregants, leaders, or the culture within that community and other communities around it.

Church hurt thus occurs when the community that is meant to be a signpost and reflection of Christ’s love becomes a place of deep wounding. Church hurt can happen in subtle ways that chip away at the foundations of relationships and in abrupt and traumatic ways as well. Something like feeling dismissed, overlooked, or unvalued can lead to church hurt, just as experiencing bullying, manipulation, or spiritual abuse can.

The pain caused by these actions is all too real. Often, the result is that the person who was hurt may become disillusioned with their faith altogether. They can begin to mistrust leadership or lose their sense of connection to the body of Christ.

The Various Paths of Church Hurt

Church hurt can come about in several ways. When Jesus was asked why He ate and spent time with unsavory characters, He responded, saying, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” (Mark 2:17, NIV) One of the main reasons why church hurt occurs is because churches are essentially hospitals full of desperately sick people in need of a savior. Church is a community of imperfect people.

The church is a community of people who have been rescued from themselves through Christ and given new lives empowered by the Holy Spirit (Colossians 3:1-17; Ephesians 2:1-10; Romans 8).

Believers are saved by the unmerited favor of God and called to a new way of life. However, Christians are still human, struggling with old patterns of sin and harmful behaviors. These are to be put to death, and that highlights the ongoing challenge that they are for believers.

Misuse of authority is a major cause of church hurt. That includes leaders behaving in domineering, abusive, and controlling ways that betray trust and misrepresent Jesus. Abuse can be physical, sexual, financial, emotional, and spiritual in nature. Whatever form it takes, it’s a leader misusing their position and damaging others along the way.

Relationships can be deeply damaged in the church because of harsh judgment and gossip. Divisive words spoken outright or behind people’s backs can erode the cohesion of a church community, and being judgmental can demean others and leave them feeling isolated.

There is a vast difference between speaking truth to one another in love (Ephesians 4:11-16) and holding each other accountable and standing in haughty judgment of one another (Galatians 6:1-10).

Apart from gossip and judgment, another source of church hurt is unmet expectations. It is right to expect great things from the community of God’s people. However, hurt can arise when one expects the community to meet every spiritual, physical, and emotional need perfectly.

In  the church, there will be a lot of give and take, a lot of learning and growing together. That is one reason Scripture calls us to bear with and forgive each other (Colossians 3:12-14; Ephesians 4:32).

Another common source of church hurt is when there are conflicts originating in cultural differences or doctrinal issues. As a collective of people from every nation, people, and tribe, and as the church is made up of people from every walk of life, there will be differences. These can be in worship styles, theological emphases, or church practices. When these differences are handled poorly or insensitively, things can escalate, and people can wound each other deeply.

Church hurt can be the result of intentional as well as unintentional actions, behaviors, attitudes, and postures that individuals or communities take. These can be the source of lasting pain, especially when they go unrecognized and aren’t dealt with wisely, in humility and love. The issue of distributing aid among widows threatened the early church, and thankfully, the disciples dealt wisely and swiftly with the concerns (Acts 6:1-7).

The reality of church hurt is an ever-present one. The community of God’s people needs to continuously rely on the Lord’s grace and wisdom as they pursue genuine accountability and seek restoration of what is broken.

How Church Hurt Impacts Individuals and the Community

The community of God’s people is often described as a body (Ephesians 4:1-16; 1 Corinthians 12; Colossians 3:15). That’s one reason why Paul writes that there shouldn’t be division in the body, and instead “its parts should have equal concern for each other. If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honored, every part rejoices with it.” (1 Corinthians 12:25-26, NIV) Christians often forget that they are part of Christ’s body along with others.

For individual believers, church hurt can have the effect of a loss of trust in spiritual leadership. There are probably too many stories that have been told describing the aftermath of a betrayal by a pastor or other church leader. There may be feelings of confusion, bitterness, and anger that result from church hurt. This can lead to emotional withdrawal or isolation if one doesn’t have space to process things with the community.

Another devastating result of church hurt is that it can result in questioning God’s goodness and even one’s own faith. If a church leader gaslights a congregant, for instance, the congregant may believe they are to blame and that their faith is defective in some way. It can take years to overcome this kind of damage. Some people have left the church altogether because of the deep spiritual wounds they’ve experienced.

The community is also affected by church hurt in various ways. A church may struggle to thrive in the wake of church hurt, especially if matters aren’t dealt with honestly. A culture of suspicion, fear, or division can take root and shape how people interact with one another.

If the community hardens its heart toward a particular individual, or if an individual or group of individuals is the source of hurt for the broader community, that can affect the dynamics of the community. Church hurt can weaken unity and damage the effective witness of Christ’s body. A community may struggle to regain its sense of self. When wounded members withdraw or leave the community, the sense of fellowship may suffer.

Finding Healing and Hope After Church Hurt

While it’s not quick or easy, restoration, healing, and hope are possible with the Lord’s help and presence. If you’ve experienced church hurt, the movement toward healing will involve intentional steps that include:

Acknowledge the pain The hurt exists, and you can name it along with the grief it’s caused before the Lord through lament.

Seek the Lord’s heart Spend time in Scripture and prayer to hear the Lord’s heart for His church. Ultimately, He is the head of the church (Ephesians 4:11-16), and He is building it (Matthew 16:18).

Humbly assess your own heart Hurt may be the result of others’ actions, but it is nonetheless wise to humbly examine if there are areas where you may need to take responsibility. This isn’t to excuse wrongdoing or victim-blame, but to ensure your own heart remains open, forgiving, and teachable. Jesus calls believers to remove the log from their own eye before addressing the speck in another’s (Matthew 7:3-5).

Forgive Forgiveness gives you freedom. It doesn’t mean forgetting or going back into unsafe situations, but it allows you to release resentment and entrust justice in the Lord’s hands (Romans 12:17-21).

Pursue healing and connection Finding healing may involve hard conversations with those you hurt or those who hurt you, where this is appropriate and safe. Consider re-engaging with a church community, even if it’s a different one, because we are meant to be in community with others.

Seek support Making sense of church hurt is best done in a context with trusted mature believers or with a trained and licensed Christian counselor. Your counselor can listen, pray with you, and guide you, helping to break the power of isolation and offering perspective.

With help, you can discover renewed hope and a deeper, more resilient faith. Contact our reception team or browse our online counselor directory to process the pain from church hurt.

item.title: Dealing with Anxiety in Pregnancy, Labor, and Delivery
item.description:
The birth of a child can be a time of excitement, joy, and wonder as one experiences the miracle of life. Starting from the moment of finding out one is expecting, to hearing the heartbeat for the first time, to preparing the nursery, culminating in that moment one first sees what love between two people was able to create when the baby takes their first breath. Becoming a mom/parent truly is one of the highest blessings that is even reflected in Scripture.

Children are a heritage from the Lord, offspring a reward from him. Like arrows in the hands of a warrior are children born in one’s youth. Blessed is the man whose quiver is full of them. – Psalm 127:3-4, NIV

Anxiety and Pregnancy

However, the reality is that for most, there is some level of anxiety related to the unknowns, particularly regarding the labor and delivery aspects of becoming a parent. It is only natural for one to worry about the pain and the safety/health of not only their baby, but also the woman bearing the child. A lot of this is normal and even beneficial for most mothers, prompting them to take steps to prepare for the delivery process.

Some steps women may take in preparation are finding a provider they feel comfortable with, asking questions, taking classes to learn positions and comforting measures during the labor process, reading books/listening to podcasts to know what to bring to the hospital, taking tours of the hospital to familiarize themselves with the space, and talking to other women who have been through the experience.

All of these measures are great as long as the woman understands that no matter how much research they do, questions they ask, books they read, or people they talk to, it is the norm to still feel like you aren’t prepared enough, especially when it comes to the delivery of your first child. Having a good support system to remind you of this and to continue encouraging you is crucial, especially as your due date approaches.

Unfortunately, though, there are some women who not only experience the “normal” level of worry during their pregnancy and delivery, but their anxiety reaches what we call “clinical levels.” What this means is that their anxiety is persistent and excessive to the point where it starts interfering with their daily functioning.

Clinical levels of anxiety can then turn a time in life that should be exciting and memorable into one that is daunting, overwhelming, and isolating, with women asking themselves, “Why am I not enjoying this?”

Causes of Anxiety in Pregnancy

Many factors can lead to diagnosable anxiety during pregnancy. These factors can be broken down into three categories: biological, psychological, and social/environmental.

Biological factors include:

  • A preexisting anxiety disorder or history of anxiety, depression, or other mental health conditions
  • A family history of anxiety or other mental health conditions
  • Hormonal changes that occur in pregnancy
  • High-risk pregnancy and/or pregnancy complications
  • Other medical conditions like thyroid disorders, PCOS, etc. that can affect mood and hormones
  • Medical conditions that can lead to complications in pregnancy
  • Insomnia or lack of sleep

Psychological factors include:

  • High levels of stress
  • Previous history of trauma, particularly sexual trauma
  • History of infertility, miscarriages, stillbirths
  • Previous traumatic pregnancy/birth experiences
  • Previous history of a newborn admission to the NICU (Neonatal Intensive Care Unit)

Social/Environmental factors include:

  • An unplanned/unwanted pregnancy
  • Limited social support
  • Financial stress, lack of stable housing or employment
  • Relationship/marital conflict
  • Domestic partner abuse
  • Attachment problems or strained relationships with one’s parents

Though these factors do not always lead to diagnosable anxiety during pregnancy it can put someone at higher risk. If this is the case for you, you are not alone, and there is hope. It may seem that some of these factors are out of your control; however, there are many steps you can take when it comes to this significant life event of bringing a child into the world.

Finding a mental health counselor is a great resource and means of support whether you are experiencing normal levels of worry or significant levels of anxiety during your pregnancy. Not only that, but if you are not yet pregnant but know you are at high risk, proactively seeking counseling is a great way to not only take care of yourself but also prepare yourself to be the best parent you can be for your child.

How Counseling Can Help

If you are already struggling with an anxiety disorder or other mental health condition, a counselor can help equip you with coping skills to help manage your anxiety. A counselor can also help you gain an understanding of your anxiety, including how anxiety works in your body, help you identify triggers, and provide psychoeducation about factors that may worsen your anxiety.

If you are someone who has been through significant trauma, a counselor can help you process that trauma and guide you on a path toward healing using trauma-based therapy modalities. A counselor can also help prepare you for how pregnancy and labor may trigger increased anxiety and how to manage those situations.

If you are someone who has experienced infertility, miscarriages, stillbirth, delivery trauma, or a previous newborn admission into the NICU, a counselor can help you process the grief that often comes with these experiences – grief that is not only related to the loss of a child, but also the loss of not having that smooth labor and delivery experience you had hoped for.

Often, these situations create increased fear coming into a hospital setting, and a counselor can teach you how to challenge these fears and challenge any inappropriate guilt that can also come with these experiences.

If you are someone who has an unplanned pregnancy, relationship/marital conflict, or lack of social support, a counselor can help you process your emotions regarding the unplanned pregnancy. An individual counselor can help you navigate the conflict in your relationship.

Or if your partner is open to it, a couple’s counselor could be a great resource to help equip you and your partner with communication/conflict resolution skills and be a mediator as you navigate decision-making regarding raising and caring for a child. A counselor can also help you identify ways to build your support system so that you do not feel alone during your pregnancy or delivery.

If you are someone dealing with stress or financial challenges, a counselor can help provide you with resources and stress management skills, as well as be a resource to identify possible solutions to the stressors you’re experiencing.

These are just a few of the ways a mental health counselor can help in managing anxiety in pregnancy and the delivery of a child. As a mental health counselor who also works as a labor and delivery nurse, I often see how severe anxiety can affect a woman’s delivery experience.

I am passionate about walking women through pre-pregnancy, pregnancy, labor and delivery, and postpartum stages. I love helping prepare women to take on one of the most important roles in their lives. What I have seen is that by taking the time and effort now to deal with anxiety and mental health concerns, you are, in effect, creating a significant impact not only on your children but on generations to come.

item.title: The Same Struggle, Different Signs: Anxiety and Depression in Men and Women
item.description:
Anxiety and depression don’t look the same for everyone. If you’ve ever wondered why one person’s distress looks like constant worry while another’s looks like irritability or shutting down, you’re already noticing something researchers have been studying for decades: gender plays a meaningful role in how emotional disorders are experienced and expressed.

This isn’t about stereotypes or assumptions. It’s about biology, hormones, social conditioning, and different ways men and women are taught to cope with distress. When we understand these patterns, we get better at recognizing anxiety and depression in ourselves and in the people we care about.

Women are diagnosed more often, but that’s not the whole story

Large population studies consistently show that women are diagnosed with both anxiety and depression at higher rates than men. But this doesn’t mean women are “more emotional” or that men don’t struggle. It means:

  • Women’s symptoms tend to match what the mental health field traditionally recognizes as anxiety or depression.
  • Men’s symptoms often show up in ways that don’t immediately look like emotional distress.

So, the real story isn’t “women are more anxious or depressed.” It’s “women’s distress is easier to see, and men’s distress is easier to miss.”

Behind the Scenes: What’s Going on in the Body

Research points to several biological factors that shape how anxiety and depression show up. These internal systems don’t determine destiny, but they do influence how our nervous systems respond to stress and overwhelming emotions.

Hormonal Fluctuations: Estrogen and progesterone influence stress‑response systems, which helps explain why anxiety and depression can spike during menstrual cycles, pregnancy, and perimenopause. Testosterone appears to have a modest protective effect.

Brain circuitry differences: Studies show sex‑linked differences in how the amygdala and stress‑response systems activate.

Genetic Architecture: Women show more anxiety‑related genetic variants, and depression often co‑occurs with internalizing traits like rumination and self‑criticism.

These “under the hood” factors help explain why women often experience internalizing symptoms – and why men may be more prone to externalizing patterns.

The Roles We’re Told to Play (Social Conditioning)

Biology sets the stage, but culture directs the performance.

Women are encouraged to express emotion Talking about fear, sadness, or feelings of being overwhelmed is more socially acceptable. As a result, women’s anxiety and depression often show up in ways that are easy to name: worry, panic, sadness, withdrawal.

Men are encouraged to be stoic Admitting fear or vulnerability can feel like breaking a rule. So, men’s distress often shows up sideways: irritability, overworking, risk‑taking, or emotional avoidance.

Same underlying distress  –  different socially acceptable “costumes.”

On Stage: How These Emotions Show Up

These factors shape why what we see looks different. If you’re a child of the nineties like I am, you grew up watching Monica on Friends hide anxiety through perfectionism, over functioning, and people-pleasing. She manages stress by controlling her environment, overachieving, and trying to meet everyone’s expectations. Her anxiety looks “productive,” but it’s driver by fear of failure and self-criticism.

Contrast that with a depiction of someone like Tony Stark. He externalizes his anxiety through being a workaholic, emotional avoidance, bravado, and productivity. Instead of expressing fear or vulnerability, he doubles down on control, innovation, and performance. These characters help us recognize that anxiety isn’t always panic or fear- it can look like being overly responsible, overly accommodating, or overly busy.

We see similar patterns with depression. If you have little kids, you’ve probably gone through (or are still going through) the Frozen stage. Elsa is a great example of internalizing depression, the form more commonly seen in women. Her emotional distress turns inward: isolation, shame, fear of being a burden, and a deep sense of not belonging.

So, she withdraws from relationships, suppresses her feelings, and carries her pain alone. Men, on the other hand, tend to externalize depression. Here, grief and hopelessness can be expressed through emotional suppression, detachment, or even risk-taking. Instead of slowing down, they might throw themselves into danger, productivity, and control.

Seeing Your Performance More Clearly

Understanding these patterns isn’t about diagnosing yourself or fitting into a category. It’s about finally recognizing the ways your own “performance” on stage may have been shaped by things happening behind the scenes- biology, expectations, and the roles you were taught to play.

So, let’s slow down and look at your performance more clearly.

Get curious about how distress shows up

  • When you’re overwhelmed, do you shut down or speed up?
  • Do you get quieter, or do you get busier?
  • Do you feel everything intensely, or do you feel nothing at all?

Ask questions you may not be used to asking

Instead of “Am I anxious?” or “Am I depressed?” try asking:

  • Do I get irritable or short when I’m overwhelmed?
  • Do I feel constantly on edge, even when I might be functioning well?
  • Do I worry about being a burden or disappointing people?
  • Do I feel like I must hold everything together, so nothing falls apart?

These questions help you see what’s happening beneath the performance- the part that often gets missed.

Notice the story you were taught about emotions

Were you taught to be the strong one? The responsible one? The easy one? The one who doesn’t make waves? Or were you taught to be accommodating, pleasant, and self‑sacrificing? Those roles shape how you show distress – and how you hide it.

Pay attention to the moments when you feel out of character

Maybe you’re the dependable one, but lately you’re exhausted. Maybe you’re the calm one, but lately you’re snapping at people. Maybe you’re the high‑achiever, but lately everything feels heavy. Those shifts are often the first signs that something deeper is happening backstage.

Let this be an invitation, not a diagnosis

You don’t have to decide today whether you’re anxious or depressed. You don’t have to fit neatly into a category or have to have the “right” symptoms. You must notice what’s happening inside you – and consider that your distress might be showing up in ways you weren’t taught to recognize.

When the Curtain Falls

There’s a moment- sometimes quiet, sometimes overwhelming- when the performance stops. When the curtain falls, and you’re no longer playing the role you’ve been handed. When the audience disappears, and it’s just you, standing in the wings, feeling the weight of what you’ve been carrying.

Maybe you’ve realized you’re exhausted from holding everything together. Maybe you’ve noticed that no matter how much you achieve, it never feels like enough. Maybe you’ve caught yourself chasing a version of peace that always seems one step out of reach. Maybe you’re starting to see that the role you’ve been performing doesn’t match what’s happening inside you, and this is exactly why it matters that anxiety and depression look different in everyone.

Because if you’ve spent years looking for the “classic” symptoms, you may have missed your own. You may have dismissed irritability as stress, overworking as responsibility, numbness as burnout, people‑pleasing as personality. You may have believed you were fine simply because your distress didn’t look like the version you were taught to expect.

Seeing your performance more clearly helps you recognize what’s been happening backstage – the tension, the overwhelming stress, the emptiness, the pressure – not as personal failures, but as signals that something in you is asking to be understood. And when you reach this place, that’s the part of the story where things can finally begin to shift. When the curtain falls, that’s where the real work begins- and where real relief becomes possible.

item.title: What Does Forgiveness Mean If You Are Stuck in Trauma?
item.description:
You hear the word used in relation to healing, and you know that unforgiveness is like a poison, but what does forgiveness mean when you strip away all of the clichés and shallow advice? If it were so easy to do, then why do people struggle with it so much? Surely there are steps or stages to forgiveness, just as there are with grief or addiction?

The truth is that forgiveness is probably a lot different from the things people have said it is. Forgiveness is not a choice you make once and try to stick to. In fact, it has nothing to do with your mentality or mindset. It is about changing your relationship to the person who hurt you, or changing your life until you can face them again.

Forgiveness is something you do to release your nervous system from being stuck in trauma. As long as you are holding onto the memory of what you experienced, your nervous system is kept in survival mode. This results in using all of your physical energy to protect you from a danger that is no longer present. Forgiveness and healing go together and cannot be separated, but the path to both might be different from what you have been taught.

What does forgiveness mean?

Forgiveness happens in your body. The emotions you feel are an echo of something happening in your body. Your nervous system feels everything you do. Anxiety can feel like a tightness in your chest, sadness like a lump in your throat, anger like a heat that flushes your face, and exhaustion like a tension in your shoulders.

When you experience the emotions caused by unforgiveness, like bitterness, resentment, fury, and disbelief, your nervous system remains activated and ready to face the threat that it thinks is causing you to feel these things. You know that these events are in the past, but your nervous system never got the memo. It responds to all these memories, emotions, and triggers as if they were a present danger.

Each time you remember the person who hurt you, or the events that traumatized you, it is a signal to your nervous system that it must fight, escape, shut down temporarily, or try to figure out a way to avoid the pain. It is like being haunted by a ghost that cannot physically harm you except by the anxiety and distress its presence causes you. As long as these events are being replayed in your memories, they are a present threat to your body.

What does forgiveness mean? Forgiveness means giving your nervous system a chance to relax. It is the act of moving to a place that is not haunted by the past and getting a good night’s sleep for the first time in years.

Forgiveness only involves you

If you were waiting to forgive that person only after they made an apology, offered an olive branch, or simply acknowledged their actions, you might wait forever. You don’t need their participation to forgive them.

It’s painful to realize that they have no plans to try to salvage the relationship or take ownership of their part in what happened. When you realize that you need to move on for your own good, even if that means you will never get an apology or acknowledgment, you have begun the healing process.

Forgiveness only waits on you alone. You might not feel ready to let things go because it takes a long time to heal from injustice. Your tormentor only has enough power over you as you give them, though. Forgiveness happens in your body and according to your own timeline. What does forgiveness mean if not healing simply because you deserve to?

Healing comes before forgiveness

The most traumatic event in your life has happened, and it has altered events for good. It was unfair, it was brutal, and it caused some serious damage that will take years to recover from. Forgiving the person who did this to you does not mean that you have to overlook this damage. In fact, it is only once you begin healing the harm that was done that you can begin forgiving the one who did it. First comes healing, then comes forgiveness.

You can choose to forgive someone because you know it’s the right thing to do, and you can say all the appropriate words to formalize your decision. Forgiveness isn’t as simple as making the choice or doing the right thing, though.

You can choose to forgive them, mentally release them, and even genuinely pray for their well-being, but until your nervous system has processed the trauma and begun healing, you cannot truly forgive or forget. What does forgiveness mean? It means giving yourself the time to heal and process the trauma so that you can move on.

Releasing the Debt

Have you ever noticed how much of the language we use to talk about forgiveness mirrors the things we say about money? We say, “they owe me an apology”, or, “I would feel better if I could get some payback.” When Jesus taught his disciples how to pray, He linked forgiveness with money debts, later translated as trespasses or sins. What does forgiveness mean? It is letting someone off the hook even while they still owe you an apology or explanation for their actions.

Forgiving someone does not mean they are welcome back into your life, or that you must fix your relationship with them. It means that you no longer owe each other anything; you are both free. Most of the time, this is why we don’t want to forgive someone: we want them to pay for what they did. When you release the charge you have over them, it completely severs the connection between you, regardless of what they meant to you before.

You are connected to someone as long as you feel like they owe you something. Forgiveness means letting go and ending that connection, even though you might never get that apology, acknowledgment, or explanation. You have lost out on those things, but you have provided yourself with closure and the freedom to move on.

True Forgiveness, Freedom, and Healing

You can choose to forgive someone over and over again, but it is only when you have properly processed your experience that you can truly forgive someone. When you have felt the anger, found the depths of your grief, and found the safety that your nervous system has been craving, you can finally and fully forgive and move on. The beauty and frustration of this experience is that it happens when it happens.

At some point, you realize that something has shifted, and you don’t feel that weight on your chest anymore, or your mind is quieter. It is like noticing that the sun has been shining for a while and smelling the gentle fragrance of new blossoms through the open window. Healing comes as unexpectedly as springtime.

If you work on processing the trauma you went through, at some point, you will no longer flinch when you hear their name, and you will look forward to a new chapter in your future. You cannot decide when you will heal. You can only begin paying attention to your needs and trying to look after yourself. What does forgiveness mean? It means doing the best for yourself and waiting for healing.

We can do a lot of work on our own, but it’s always better when we have others helping us. We host an online catalog of counselors where you can find someone to begin meeting with if you want some extra support. Our reception team would also be happy to help you find the right person for you. Healing and forgiveness are hard and complicated, but you don’t have to be alone on the journey.

item.title: Anger at the Wheel: Signs of an Anger Issue
item.description:
Sometimes, the small things can be indicators of bigger things to come, and what seems innocuous can turn out to be problematic later. Signs of an anger issue might be small or subtle, but they shouldn’t be ignored. When the space shuttle Challenger had an issue with small rubber O-rings (simple circular seals around the diameter of a coin), it led to disaster for the entire crew. Similarly, anger can overthrow a person’s life, causing a lot of damage.

Is anger good or bad?

The word anger might bring up specific images for you. This could be culled from media or perhaps from real-life experiences that you’ve had. Anger is a lot of things, but quite often anger looks and feels ugly. It’s the sort of emotion that might pull us in, but it leaves regret in its wake. Most of us have experienced anger in ourselves or from others, and it’s the sort of experience we’d rather avoid. Anger leaves a bad taste in one’s mouth.

It’s important to remember that anger is a God-given emotion. Like all things the Lord has given us, anger can be turned to ungodly purposes. This doesn’t alter the fact that anger is part of our makeup, and that’s how we were designed. In its proper place, anger alerts us to things being out of alignment, whether that’s injustice, personal boundaries being violated, or because loved ones are in danger of harm and need protection.

Scripture acknowledges anger, and we find Jesus feeling angry at willful blindness as in Mark 3:1-6, for example. There is such a thing as righteous anger, which is anger aroused by an appropriate object or situation and expressed appropriately in turn. God is angry about sin because of how it damages us and the world around us. His anger moves Him to act lovingly, justly, and graciously about that sin.

There is a difference between anger as an emotion, along with the right uses of that anger, and what happens when anger masters you. When anger crosses the line and stops being something that you feel, instead becoming something that rules over or controls you, anger is no longer serving the purpose the Lord set for it. That is when anger erodes relationships, peace, health, and even spiritual witness.

So, is anger good or bad? It’s a bit simplistic putting things that way, but we can talk about it by saying: it depends. Anger can be a good thing when that anger is doing what it is supposed to, but it can also be bad when it gets out of hand and isn’t expressed appropriately.

When anger is in control, it’s dangerous for everyone around you, including yourself. The problem with anger and anger issues is that they are sometimes subtle and don’t announce themselves as we would imagine. That’s why it’s important to know the signs of an anger issue.

The Signs of an Anger Issue

Anger can be subtle, and there are some behaviors that you might not even think of as angry simply because they don’t look like you think anger is supposed to look. Anger issues can creep in bit by bit. They can become normalized by habit, or over time, you can find yourself minimizing them because of feeling shame at what your anger does to you and the people around you. Some signs to look out for include:

Struggling to let things go: It’s not unheard of for someone to carry a grievance for days, weeks, months, or even years. People do cause us harm, but if you find yourself nursing a grudge, replaying offenses in your mind, or building up a mental case against the people who have wronged you, your anger has morphed from being a moment into a stronghold in your life.

Your anger is disproportionate: Being angry is one thing, but it’s important to ask if the anger matches what aroused it, and if the reaction is justified. An anger problem will often reveal itself when there is a consistent mismatch between the trigger for anger and the reaction. When small frustrations regularly produce a firestorm or resentment that lingers, it’s a sign that anger has a hold on you.

Your anger frightens others: It’s worthwhile looking within for the signs of anger issues, but other signs could come from the people around us. How others are around you tells you something important. If your children walk on eggshells around you, if your spouse is anxious in your presence, or if colleagues aren’t eager to collaborate or bring you difficult news because of how you’d react, pay attention to that.

You use anger as a tool: One of the ways anger can be abused is when it starts to function as a means of control and not just as an honest expression of feeling. Anger becomes harmful when it becomes a way of getting what you want from other people. This could look like withdrawing in a cold silence to punish someone, being intimidating to shut down conflict, or raising your voice to make others back down.

Deep regret after anger passes: The Lord made us with the capacity for remorse and to understand the impact our words and actions have on others. If you find yourself regularly making apologies and amends for things you said or did in anger, if you find yourself feeling shame for your actions, but the cycle keeps repeating like a bad dream, that pattern could be pointing to anger issues.

Do you repeatedly regret the way anger leads you to hurt others, but change isn’t forthcoming? The lack of lasting change suggests that the roots of the anger haven’t been unearthed and dealt with.

Anger is affecting your health: Anger isn’t just a mental thing, a set of thoughts roiling around inside of you. Anger is also a physical thing, and it manifests physically through things like a rapid heart rate and clenched muscles. Chronic and unmanaged anger results in tension headaches, trouble sleeping, and high blood pressure. Your body keeps score, telling you that you may have anger issues.

Unhealthy coping mechanisms: The healthy way to deal with anger is to express it in a calm, clear manner that doesn’t blame, shame, or harm others. Suppressing anger, letting anger explode, being passive-aggressive, or directing the anger at yourself are all unhealthy ways of expressing anger. Some people turn to alcohol, food, overwork, or other numbing behaviors to deal with anger, and this isn’t healthy.

Turning to these and other behaviors after an angry episode or when you anticipate such a situation indicates that you’re feeling angry but not processing it properly. Not facing your anger and processing it is a sign that you may have anger issues.

What to Do with Signs of Anger Issues

If you encounter these signs of anger issues in your life, what comes next? For one thing, recognizing these signs shouldn’t be cause for shame. When we fall short, one common response is to withdraw into ourselves or try to hide those shortcomings, perhaps even from ourselves. We might even deflect and try to blame others for it. It’s certainly what the first humans did (Genesis 3:7-13).

Instead of withdrawing, deflecting, or denying, seeing these signs should be seen as an invitation to healing. The Lord wants us to be whole. He wants our lives to be lives of abundant joy, peace, love, patience, self-control, and a lot of other amazing things that are good for us and for the world (Galatians 5:22-26). You don’t have to navigate this journey alone. Christian counseling for anger can be your courageous first step.

Christian counseling for anger can offer you an opportunity and space to work through the roots of your anger. Anger is often not the core issue that’s affecting you; it may be a symptom of deeper wounds such as grief, past trauma, unmet needs, or fear. Counseling is a space where compassion, honesty, and grace are at the foundation, and those wounds can be tended to.

Help is available. You can reach out to our office or browse our online counselor directory to take anger out of the driver’s seat and start moving toward healing and wholeness.

item.title: Anxiety Reduction for First Responders: Finding Peace in High-Pressure Roles
item.description:
The stressors that first responders face are unique to their careers. Their work demands that they be consistently vigilant, quick to make decisions, and emotionally resilient as they face situations where lives are at stake.

Along with this dedication come the challenges that accumulate emotionally and mentally. We don’t always see the internal struggles first responders face daily. Anxiety reduction is vital to helping these individuals maintain focus and clarity as they serve effectively.

The process of managing anxiety includes the acknowledgment that these pressures are real and that seeking support is not a sign of weakness. Intentional strategies that will address anxiety are required for first responders to avoid burnout, compassion fatigue, and diminished capacity to respond effectively in the critical moments of their daily work.

Scripture reminds us that we can come to God with everything we think and feel. “Be anxious for nothing, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God.” (Philippians 4:6, NASB) This is true for first responders, too.

The Hidden Weight of Constant Readiness

First responders are required to maintain a high-alert mindset. They need to be ready to respond at any moment. This often means that their nervous systems rarely experience true rest. Their daily life has a perpetual readiness woven into every minute, making it difficult to distinguish between on-duty and off-duty.

When the brain adapts to this pattern, there are consequences. Sleep disturbance, irritability, and difficulty relaxing are common experiences that first responders must navigate. Christian counselors understand this hypervigilance and can help navigate intentional counterbalancing practices that allow the body and mind to rest.

There is an unspoken message that surrounds first responders as they absorb the cultural message regarding their profession. That message is that first responders are unshakeable and that displaying any emotional response somehow makes them less able to do their job. This expectation conflicts with human neurobiology. When individuals are repeatedly exposed to traumatic situations, it affects them and everyone around them.

This cultural expectation results in first responders feeling as though they must maintain an image of invulnerability as they struggle with anxiety, intrusive thought patterns, and emotional exhaustion. The disconnect between what they experience internally and what they feel they are permitted to express externally creates additional strain, complicating and compounding the existing stress.

First responders can lean on the promise that “The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit.” (Psalm 34:18, NASB) They don’t need to hide their struggles from Him.

Anxiety Reduction Through Practical Mental Health Strategies

There are specific anxiety-reduction techniques that can benefit first responders when integrated into their daily routine. One effective technique is box breathing, also known as tactical breathing. This breathing technique involves counting to four as the individual inhales, holding for a count of four, exhaling for a count of four, and holding again for a count of four. This can be a real-time tool because it is simple and accessible.

Another technique that can be helpful in anxiety reduction for first responders is progressive muscle relaxation. This helps first responders identify where they are holding tension in their bodies and consciously release it.

Establishing boundaries between work and personal life is a foundation for long-term anxiety management. This requires the individual to create a ritual that signals transitions, such as changing clothes immediately after shifts or engaging in brief physical activity.

These practices can help the nervous system reset and understand that danger has passed and safety has returned. Christian counselors help first responders understand that these boundaries honor their calling to serve and the need to preserve their own well-being.

Sabbath rest speaks directly to the need for rhythms that include cessation from work. When first responders choose to step away from their responsibilities for intentional rest, they are modeling the biblical principle that rest is required to sustain effectiveness. Jesus calls us to Him for rest when we are weary. “Come to Me, all who are weary and heavy-laden, and I will give you rest.” (Matthew 11:28, NASB)

The Role of Connection and Community

First responders often feel isolated because they cannot share their experiences with people outside their field. Having a peer support group that allows them to share with others who understand gives them a space for honest conversation. These connections remind them that their responses are normal reactions to abnormal circumstances. When they gather with others who understand the unique pressures of their work, the weight of carrying these experiences alone begins to diminish.

Engaging in professional mental health support tailored for first responders can offer a crucial layer of care. Therapists and counselors who specialize in trauma and occupational stress understand the specific challenges involved with being a first responder. Through evidence-based treatments integrated with faith-based support, a way to address trauma symptoms directly is created.

Engaging with this professional support demonstrates wisdom rather than weakness. It shows a commitment to maintaining the capacity to serve in the long term. The decision to seek professional help allows first responders to process what they have experienced during their shifts in a safe environment where their vulnerability is respected, and healing is prioritized.

Working with a Christian counselor embodies the directive in Ecclesiastes. “Two are better than one because they have a good return for their labor. For if either of them falls, the one will lift up his companion.” (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10, NASB) A counselor can be there to support first responders in their struggles.

Physical Health as a Foundation for Anxiety Reduction

The connection between physical health and mental well-being is particularly important for first responders. Regular exercise can provide a healthy outlet for processing stress and hormones and improve overall resilience to anxiety. Cardiovascular exercise, strength training, and flexibility all contribute to better stress regulation. First responders often find that establishing a consistent exercise routine creates structure and predictability for those with unpredictable schedules.

First responders have irregular schedules that often disrupt their sleep patterns, which impacts anxiety levels. When first responders are able to maintain consistent sleep at night by creating dark, cool sleep environments, they can improve their sleep quality even with their challenging schedules.

Eating balanced meals to stabilize blood sugar prevents symptoms of anxiety from compounding the mental and emotional load. These practical steps create a foundation that supports anxiety reduction and helps first responders maintain the physical stamina their work demands. They can care for their body as the temple God says it is to help them withstand the challenges of their work.

Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own? – 1 Corinthians 6:19, NASB

Sustainable Service Through Self-Care

First responders are professionals whose work holds immense value. They choose to protect and serve communities in the most vulnerable moments. But sustaining the service throughout their careers requires acknowledging that even the strongest individual needs support.

Anxiety reduction involves developing practices and support systems that prevent anxiety from becoming overwhelming and debilitating. Christian counselors work with first responders to create personalized approaches that will honor their professional calling and the human need for care.

Navigating toward better mental health in the demanding roles of first responders starts with recognizing that seeking help reflects strength and wisdom. This requires implementing practical strategies and addressing deeper patterns of thought and belief that influence how first responders relate to their experiences.

Faith offers a framework for understanding that human limitations are part of the design, and a reminder that dependence on God isn’t weakness but the pathway to enduring strength. When first responders prioritize their mental health through anxiety-reduction practices, they are positioning themselves to serve more effectively and sustainably.

If you are a first responder struggling with anxiety, we encourage you to reach out to a Christian counselor who understands the unique demands of your profession. You can call our reception team or use the contact form to get started on your journey to reduce anxiety.

item.title: Overcoming the Challenges of Being a Stepparent In a Blended Family
item.description:
The word “family” can conjure up wildly different pictures and emotions for different people. Your experience of family shapes what you expect and desire regarding family. These experiences will vary, as some families have one parent or none; a person may be an only child or have many siblings; and the home that one grows up in might be a happy and healthy one, but it can also be extremely dysfunctional.

One family situation that you could find yourself part of is a blended family. This comes with its own set of blessings and challenges.

Different Family Dynamics and Difficulties Within Blended Families

Families come in all shapes and sizes, and that includes blended families. A blended family is when two people form a new family with kids from previous situations. A new family is forged out of two or more previously separate families. The children that form this new family might have been adopted, from previous partners, or born to the couple, or a combination of the above.

Family dynamics are complex enough when everyone is related by blood and part of the same household from the beginning. The impact of dynamics such as birth order can affect how siblings understand themselves and their role in the family. When two families come together, not only do the joys multiply, but these complex dynamics of interaction multiply, too.

Blended families are often faced with unique challenges that can test bonds and the ingenuity of parents in navigating those new family dynamics. As stepparents, there are a few common challenges to be aware of that can affect how family members relate to one another.

Common challenges

Grief and Loss The new family may come in the wake of broken relationships, and family members may still be grieving the loss of those previous relationships, or they may need time to adjust to new family dynamics. Grief is a complex process, and each family member may be experiencing and expressing it differently.

Communication Issues As the new family gets to know each other, there may be difficulties with communication. Between different communication styles and expectations, it’s easy for misunderstandings and conflicts to occur and escalate. These can erode the sense of connection between family members.

Making Necessary Adjustments When the new family comes together, it can take time for family members to make the required adjustments to their new roles, responsibilities, and relationships. Perhaps your child was the oldest or only child, and now they have new older siblings, and it can take time to come to terms with these changes.

Forming Bonds As with any relationship, it takes time and effort to build strong relationships between step-siblings and stepparents.

Co-parenting The parents in this situation may not approach parenting in the same way. The couple who formed the blended family may each have different parenting styles, and the other biological parents of those children may also have their own parenting philosophy, which can lead to conflicts and challenges in co-parenting.

Financial Stress Bringing two families together can bring financial stress as both families make financial adjustments, such as different or increased expenses or shifts in financial priorities. The lifestyle that the family can maintain might change, which can add stress of its own.

Social Stigma Blended families, particularly ones where the differences are visible, often unfortunately face societal stigma or judgment. This may affect a family member’s self-esteem and confidence.

Scheduling and Logistics A bigger family with different needs will often result in complexities when coordinating schedules, routines, and daily life.

Conflicting Loyalties Another common challenge is that children may feel as though they need to make a choice, and they can be torn in their affections or allegiances between their biological parents and stepparents, leading to feelings of guilt or conflicted loyalties. This can be especially pronounced if the parents take sides and encourage the children to do the same.

Different Family Cultures Blending families can lead to a clash due to differences in values, traditions, and expectations. These differences may be rooted in the different cultural backgrounds of the family, or they can stem from the fact that families will often have certain ways of doing things. For example, some families are tight-knit and spend the holidays together, or they are quite outdoorsy, while other families are spread out and prefer indoor activities.

Every family is unique in its strengths, capacities, story, and the resources available to them. The challenges that each blended family faces will vary, but these challenges can be overcome. By employing open communication, empathy, compassion, and patience with one another, a family can navigate these challenges well and build a strong, loving family bond.

Overcoming Challenges Within Blended Families

When you’re a stepparent in a blended family, the challenges that you’ll face can be complex and deep. However, these difficulties can be faced squarely, and you can overcome them. With dedication, empathy, patience, and wisdom, you can implement some of the following strategies to knit your new family together in authentic and loving relationships.

Communicate openly It’s important for everyone to be on the same page, or at least be aware of each other. Be sure to talk to your partner, stepchildren, and their biological parents, if they are involved, to understand any feelings and concerns that they may have. It’s important to know what expectations they may have, as well as how they conduct relationships.

Set clear boundaries While it’s important to understand where everyone stands, you have your boundaries, as does every family member. Establishing clear rules and expectations will help you avoid confusion and resentment, which often comes when there isn’t clarity. Without clear boundaries, relationships and tempers may get frayed. Setting boundaries also means carving space to perform self-care.

Build your relationships gradually You and your stepchildren may not connect instantaneously. Relationships take time to develop, so take that time to develop healthy and positive connections with your stepchildren, making sure to respect their boundaries and individual needs along the way.

In line with this, be patient and flexible, keeping in mind that blended families can be complex, so you’ll need to be prepared for that and prepared to adapt and adjust as you go along.

As you build your relationships gradually, show love and consistency, particularly when it comes to enforcing rules and their consequences. Don’t be partial to your biological children, and provide a stable, loving environment for the whole family.

Support the parent-child relationship Make sure that you encourage a healthy relationship between your partner and the children, avoiding competition or interference. This can include taking steps to respect their authority and not undermining their decisions or authority, even when you disagree. You and your partner should talk about your expectations as well as how you’ll parent the children.

A blended family works best when both partners have a healthy respect for each other and are mutually supportive in parenting and other decisions. Fostering a positive co-parenting relationship will entail working with your partner to present a united front so that you’re not playing favorites.

Create a new family culture and traditions Being a blended family provides an amazing opportunity to bring together the best qualities of both families. Nurture special traditions or family rituals that promote a sense of unity and belonging in the family. For instance, celebrate milestones and successes together through special meals or outings.

Seek professional help Being a blended family has its joys, but it does have unique challenges. If these challenges persist, consider family therapy or counseling to help you address issues and strengthen your relationships.

Counseling can help you discover, emphasize, and use your strengths to foster deeper bonds and overcome issues such as poor communication or disconnectedness. With help, your family can be the loving, nurturing, and supportive environment you desire it to be. Contact our office today to schedule your first risk-free appointment.
