item.title: How to Improve Communication in a Relationship in a Digital World
item.description:
Communication is important in every aspect of life. It’s so important that entire college degrees are centered on communication. Psychologists work carefully with clients to help them learn how to be more effective communicators, and multi-million dollar business deals rely on it. The world of art centers on conveying ideas through visual presentation.

Even the Bible talks about communication and how it affects our lives. It talks about the importance of speaking the truth and helping to build each other up (Ephesians 4:15, Ephesians 4:29). It tells us to be quick to listen and describes the fallout when we don’t (James 1:19, Proverbs 27:6).

It’s clear that communicating ideas effectively is important for nearly every facet of life, but it’s particularly important in relationships. Even if your communication isn’t the best, you can learn how to improve communication in a relationship.

Shouldn’t Communication Be Improving?

One would think that with all the connectivity that our modern age affords us, communication would be improving. Unfortunately, that is simply not true. Modern conveniences like texting and email may provide us with instant access to the people in our lives, but it doesn’t guarantee quality communication.

Texting

Much of our modern conversations happen through texting. While texting allows people to stay in touch more easily, it also undermines the authentic beauty of face-to-face communication. And texting can often cause a lack of clarity in content and intent.

The nuances of in-person conversations, the flicker of the eyes, micro-facial expressions, and voice inflections are all gone when communication is reduced to words on a screen. Even though the use of emojis can give more clarity and context than words alone, there is still a discrepancy between the effectiveness of in-person communication and what is done over text.

Out of Practice

Not only does this texting deteriorate the quality of communication, but it can also affect your ability to communicate in general. Just like all other skills, communication is a learned skill that needs to be practiced to be perfected. When texting and other digital means become the main source of communication, your ability to interact in person can suffer.

Avoidance

Most people will avoid conflict when they can, and the internet affords you that luxury. It’s often easier to avoid difficult conversations by leaving people “on read” or ghosting them entirely than it is to have a conflict. Because the internet allows physical distance in communication, it enables you to avoid conversations that really should take place.

Misunderstandings

Many conflicts and misunderstandings, even broken relationships, could be avoided if people were simply willing to say what they actually mean and actively listen to one another. Misunderstandings abound online where tone and intent are easily misread. Without the benefit of facial expressions, body language, and even voice inflections, it’s tempting for your audience to fill in the gap in communication with their own assumptions.

How to Improve Communication

The good news is that communication is a skill. Like any other skill, it can be improved with practice and intentional effort, even in the digital age.

Be Quick to Listen

Scripture says to be “quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to become angry” (James 1:19, NIV). When you actively listen, you’re allowing the person you’re talking with to feel heard, and that builds trust. To do this in a practical sense, you should prioritize in-person conversations over digital communication and put away your device when you do. This helps you give your full attention to the person in front of you.

If you’re communicating digitally, you can still be an active listener by fully reading text or comments rather than skimming for important information and perhaps missing important details in the process.

Speak Clearly

Saying what you mean in a kind and respectful, even direct way helps to eliminate confusion and reduces the chance of hurt feelings. Avoid vague or passive language and get into the habit of using concise words to express your thoughts in a way that leaves no room for confusion.

Be Honest

While it seems like speaking honestly should go without saying, a lack of authenticity can deteriorate friendships and shut communication down. Ephesians 4 encourages believers to speak the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15, NIV). While honesty is the expectation in communication, it should also be tempered with love.

Being honest also requires you to be vulnerable. Digital communication can act as a shield sometimes. It allows you to curate a version of yourself that is filtered and edited, void of authenticity. Later in the fourth chapter of Ephesians, we’re told to “put off falsehood” (Ephesians 4:25, NIV). In this context, it shows that we must be willing to share ourselves with others in an unedited, unfiltered state.

Address Issues Directly

Matthew 18:15 shows the importance of going directly to someone when there’s a problem instead of allowing anger and resentment to fester or manifest in a less healthy way. This is a good practice in the modern world, too.

Don’t allow issues to grow or involve other people unnecessarily. In the digital world, it can be tempting to ignore issues or to vent online. But part of being honest is also going directly to the person you have an issue with, rather than allowing that issue to be aired online in a public forum or ignoring the issue altogether.

Practice Patience

If you’re a Christ-follower, you know all about grace and patience. God extended it to you when you accepted Christ, and He continues to forgive, over and over again. The Bible calls us to do the same: “Bear with each other and forgive one another.” (Colossians 3:13, NIV) You will inevitably have misunderstandings and bad communication days. But you can consciously choose patience instead of reactionary behavior to help mitigate the negative effects.

Make Echoing a Habit

Implement active verification into your communication to ward off misunderstandings. In person, you probably do this naturally with a nod of your head or the occasional “uh-huh.” But online, you have to do it manually.

Before you react to a text that feels potentially hurtful, ask for clarification. Ask something like, “Am I understanding correctly that you…” Not only does this demand clarification, but this small pivot in the conversation helps you to practice being slow to anger.

Don’t Blame Technology Entirely

While it’s easy to blame modern communication problems on the internet, the truth is that, while online communication does have its limitations, it’s not entirely to blame. Technology doesn’t create communication flaws; it just amplifies them.

A smartphone doesn’t make you a reactionary person. It just gives you the tools to act on your reactions and may amplify the effect. If you struggle with honesty, the internet may give you a convenient and easy platform on which to deceive. Consider how you use technology and why. This will help clarify what lies beneath your digital communications.

Adhere to the Two Text Rule

Some conversations are just too complicated or important to take place over text. A rule to follow for relationships is that if a disagreement or a complex topic isn’t resolved in two text exchanges, the conversation should be moved immediately to a voice call or in person conversation. This prevents assumptions from being made.

Therapy Can Help You Improve Communication in Your Relationships

If you need help learning how to be a better communicator, make an appointment with one of our Christian therapists today. Sometimes an outside perspective can make it easier to recognize patterns in your own life, which can help you find healthier ways to express your emotions and thoughts. In therapy, you can also learn how to be a better listener and how to overcome any habits that might be interfering with your communication.

Digital communication is faster, but not necessarily better. Technology may shape how you communicate, but it doesn’t change the importance of listening well, speaking the truth, and treating others with kindness. Words matter, even if they are just on a screen.

Connect with this office for a risk-free consultation to see how Christian therapy can help you improve your communication.

item.title: How to Soothe the Fight, Flight, Freeze, and Fawn Response
item.description:
Fight, flight, freeze, and fawn are commonly known as stress responses. The nervous system activates this response to protect you from danger. Unfortunately, due to daily stressors, our minds and bodies now assume danger in anything that causes worry or stress. We no longer fear apex predators; we are anxious about mortgages or rent, utilities, car payments, medical bills, student loans, work, and relationships.

The body responds to these stimuli by activating the sympathetic nervous system, eliciting one or more of these responses.

Understanding the responses

Understanding the responses can lead to better managing the experience when activated. While the fight, flight, and freeze responses have been known for some time, the fawn response is newer and comes from the study of nervous system responses.

Each response is the body’s way of trying to protect itself and presents differently for everyone. However, each response has common experiences. The fight response does not always mean fight in a physical sense. It can look like being irritable, defensive, feeling anger, and/or aggression.

The flight response can look like avoiding, panicking, chronic worry, and/or wanting to run away or flee. The freeze response can look like depression, feeling stuck, dissociation, feeling like your mind “goes blank,” feeling confused, and/or being passive. The fawn response can look like avoiding conflict, people-pleasing (or codependency), and/or difficulty with setting healthy boundaries.

All of these responses are not necessarily unhealthy. Most of them can be helpful when the situation requires it. When there is continuous or constant activation, it can lead to unhelpful or unhealthy experiences.

Why the Sympathetic Nervous System Cannot Stay Stuck in Overdrive

The sympathetic nervous system can get stuck due to chronic stress or severe trauma. When the stress response kicks into overdrive, you can experience physical, emotional, and mental issues.

Chronic stress can cause the following symptoms and conditions (and is not exhaustive):

  • Chronic high blood pressure
  • Increased risk of heart disease
  • Rapid heart rate or palpitations
  • Tension headaches
  • Unexplained aches and pains
  • Digestive problems, like Irritable Bowel Syndrome
  • Heartburn and acid reflux
  • Dizziness and fatigue
  • Weight changes
  • Appetite changes
  • Sleep issues
  • Higher risk for Type 2 diabetes
  • Anxiety disorders
  • Depressive disorders
  • Weakened immune system

The body attempts to compensate by maintaining the mode (fight, flight, freeze, or fawn). The most effective way to mitigate these stress responses is to activate the parasympathetic nervous system to calm the mind and body.

Soothing the Fight, Flight, or Fawn Response Immediately

Heightened anxiety and panic attacks, the results of an overactive nervous system response, can seem scary and interfere with your daily activities. When stress triggers a response, you need a method or strategies to help ground you in the present and bring your nervous system back into alignment.

The following methods can help soothe these responses. Practice each one several times to see how it works for your situation. The more often you use the strategies, the easier they will be to remember.

5-4-3-2-1 Grounding Technique

The 5-4-3-2-1 grounding technique is a simple activity that uses the five senses to keep you in the present and help calm anxious thoughts. With this method, you must concentrate on the items in your environment. You can implement this technique when you feel anxious or at the start of a panic attack.

Take note of your environment. Name five things you see, four things you can touch, three things you can hear, two things you can smell, and one thing you can taste. Take your time noticing each of the five senses. Note the texture of an item or the aroma.

Deep Breathing

Deep breathing activates the parasympathetic nervous system, thereby slowing the heart and respiratory rates. When people become panicked, they tend to breathe more shallowly and faster as they prepare to protect themselves from danger. Unfortunately, this reaction can make you feel dizzy and out of control. Deep breathing regulates these processes.

Try a simple deep breathing exercise. One exercise is the box breathing, which can be done by inhaling deeply through the nose for the count of four. Hold the breath for four to seven beats, and then exhale through the mouth for the count of four to eight.

Another breathing exercise is to inhale deeply through your nose for four seconds, hold for seven seconds, and exhale for eleven seconds. Both exercises can be repeated as necessary. As you inhale, feel your lungs expand to maximize benefit.

Dive Reflex

The dive reflex is elicited by submerging the face in cold water or by splashing cold water on the face, thereby activating the vagus nerve. The vagus nerve is part of the parasympathetic nervous system, also referred to as the rest-and-digest system. This nervous system regulates breathing, heart rate, blood pressure, and digestive function.

To activate the vagus nerve with the dive reflex, submerge your face in cold water for about 30 seconds, ensuring that the skin around your nose and under your eyes is covered. If you would prefer not to submerge your face, you can use a cold pack or a very cold washcloth to cover the areas. Consult a physician before attempting the dive reflex if you have cardiac issues.

Humming a Tune

Have you ever heard someone hum when stressed? Perhaps they were working behind the counter in a busy store or pharmacy, humming while working quickly. Humming activates the vagus nerve through the vibrations coming from the throat. Some people find that humming a tune or singing helps them relax when they are anxious.

When you hum, make sure you can feel the vibration in your throat. You can also make more of a buzzing sound. This vibration “wakes” up the vagus nerve. Most people don’t notice humming, especially when the radio is on or in a hectic crowd, such as while shopping.

Shifting Out of the Freeze Response

Learning to help your nervous system “thaw” and return to alignment after a freeze response will help you get back into your daily routine more quickly. The more you practice these response methods, the faster you will regain control.

Practice is progress. It may not seem that a method is working at first, but consider that even a slight improvement is better than none, and you can build on these small beginnings.

Take Note of Your Environment

During a freeze response, your mind may “zoom” out. You need to “zoom” back into focus by taking note of your environment. Look around and use the 5-4-3-2-1 technique, if possible. Suppose you cannot, try the grounding method on a smaller scale. Reach out and touch one or two items, noting the texture. Name what you hear. Is there a scent you can identify? They now produce small tubes containing essential oils that you can sniff to activate the parasympathetic nervous system.

Make Small Movements to “Thaw”

Sometimes even the smallest movements seem monumental during the freeze response. Try micro-movements initially to help you “thaw.” For example, move your eyes around the room to take in your environment, slowly move one finger at a time, stretching each, or rub a finger against your thumb on the same hand.

Move Your Body When Ready

When you feel you can move your body, use graceful, soft movements rather than hurried reactions. Stand and stretch, move your feet in a shuffle, or do a few marches. Your mind and body are coming back into alignment and need a few minutes to catch up. Don’t try to rush it.

Long-Term Help

The most effective way to treat these responses is to prevent them through lifestyle interventions. Small changes can bring significant results. One new habit could make the next panic attack more manageable. These changes can facilitate emotion regulation, improve physical health, and manage symptoms.

Connect with Others

Anxiety and depressive disorders can keep you from wanting to spend time with others. Many people avoid locations, people, or situations that can trigger panic attacks. However, God did not create you to live in a vacuum. Socialization and connection with others can help shoulder the burden, lift mood, and nurture relationships. Choose a few trusted people to turn to when you feel anxious. Call them or invite them over for coffee or a snack.

Take Exercise Daily

Exercise is a natural anti-anxiety and anti-depressant medication. Engaging in daily exercise will improve physical health while lowering stress hormones and releasing endorphins. These endorphins and other brain chemicals boost mood and regulate emotions. Aim for at least 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity exercise (thirty minutes on five days per week). When you feel anxious, even a 10-15-minute session could relieve stress and improve your mood.

Seek Professional Help

Professional help is one of the best ways to begin the journey to managing your experience. Seeking help from a medical doctor to ensure there is not anything off or missing physically can assist in maintaining proper responses.

In the same way, seeking help from a mental health practitioner can help you get to the root of your anxiety, manage triggers and symptoms, and learn how to move forward. A counselor will customize a plan for you based on your specific circumstances and assess regularly.

Calming Stress Responses are Possible

You can regulate your body’s stress responses. It takes practice, but you can prevent and manage the freeze response as well as the fight-or-flight response. Contact our office today to consult with a Christian counselor about the best ways to lower your anxiety and worry with counseling and lifestyle interventions.

item.title: Overcoming Extreme Anxiety: Tips from a Christian Counselor in Texas
item.description:
Anxiety affects millions of people in the United States annually. Extreme anxiety can lead to physical and mental conditions, such as high blood pressure, heart disease, stomach issues, headaches, panic attacks, and unexplained aches and pains.

Extreme anxiety can interfere with your job and relationships. It can keep you from taking action on good opportunities or attending special events. Anxiety can rob you of your confidence and self-esteem.

God created your body to react to stress to protect you from danger and predators. Unfortunately, our minds perceive danger to also include stressful events or late mortgage payments. Other factors, like brain structure or function, brain chemical imbalance, genetics, family history, trauma, or environmental factors, contribute to increased levels of anxiety.

You can learn to control extreme anxiety through lifestyle changes, professional treatment, and support.

Tips for Overcoming Extreme Anxiety

Overcoming extreme anxiety means looking at the condition from all angles. You need an approach that addresses physical, emotional, mental, and spiritual health. If you rely solely on one, you risk neglecting other areas.

For example, if you concentrate on using exercise to fight anxiety and depression without addressing negative thoughts and challenging old beliefs, the thoughts will continue and fuel your anxiety.

Think of your brain like a giant computer. Anxiety is like an open tab running in the background. Perhaps you are not working on that screen currently, but it is still running and consuming power and resources from your computer. Anxiety is like that underlying tab, leaving you feeling worried, on edge, and mentally frazzled.

The following are several tips for overcoming extreme anxiety.

Seek counseling

Counseling provides the opportunity for a safe space to delve into the root of your anxiety, identify anxious thoughts, challenge negative beliefs, and learn how to reframe thoughts to result in positive outcomes.

Talk therapy is most commonly known in counseling, followed by Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT). CBT is used widely for various mental conditions. It is based on identifying and analyzing negative thoughts. These anxious thoughts influence emotions and behaviors. By changing the way we think, we increase the likelihood of feeling and acting differently.

Exposure therapy is a method that gradually introduces the client to a situation to assist in the desensitization process. For example, for clients with extreme anxiety in social situations, a counselor may suggest minimal exposure initially. This might look like a short trip to the drugstore to purchase one item or walking into a café to buy a coffee on the least busy day.

Your counselor will customize a plan for your situation and the severity of your anxiety symptoms.

Lower stress

We have all been told to manage stress, but doing it is easier said than done. Engaging in activities that lower stress will activate the parasympathetic nervous system. This lowers adrenaline and cortisol levels, and improves blood pressure and resting heart rate.

You can lower stress right away by practicing deep breathing. When you feel anxious, take a few minutes to inhale through your nose for the count of four, hold the breath for the count of four, then release through the mouth for the count of four. Repeat as necessary. Take note of any tense muscles and try to relax them as you exhale.

To lower stress for the long term, take a look at your schedule and responsibilities. Is there anything you can delegate to others or delete? Are you taking on too much? Have you set unrealistic expectations for yourself? Learn to set boundaries and say no. Prioritize tasks that align with your beliefs and values, and stop striving using your own strength. As we know, our own strength is nothing compared to God’s strength. Let Him lead you.

Make exercise a habit

Exercise lowers stress hormones and releases a flood of endorphins, serotonin, dopamine, and other neurotransmitters. This combination boosts mood, improves cognitive function, strengthens cardiovascular processes, and builds confidence.

To receive the most benefit, make exercise a part of your daily routine. It should become a habit just like brushing your teeth. If you want to make the habit stick, stack the habit onto another well-established one.

For example, stretch for 10 minutes after brushing your teeth in the morning. Or, slip your workout clothes on as soon as you arrive home after work and lift weights for 30 minutes before making dinner. You are more likely to stick with it if it’s part of your regular schedule.

Turn bedtime into a routine

Sleep should be a priority. You will have a harder time regulating emotions if you skimp on sleep. Sleep can also elude you due to anxious thoughts, making it challenging to fall and stay asleep during the night.

Create a bedtime routine to initiate sleep. For example, shower or change into pajamas after dinner to signal to your brain that it is time to unwind. Choose two or three habits you will incorporate into this routine. You could choose to turn off your devices, brew a cup of herbal tea, and read a book before bed. Choose relaxing activities. If you exercise, complete your workout at least three hours before bed, so that the endorphin rush does not interfere with sleep.

Eat healthier food

We have all heard the suggestion to eat healthier food, but we may not realize that nutrition plays a part in mental health. The foods you eat can influence how you feel. Some substances worsen anxiety and depression symptoms. Some ultra-processed foods dull cognitive function, leading to brain fog.

Aim to eat nutritious, balanced meals of lean proteins, healthy fats, complex carbohydrates, and fresh fruits and vegetables. Avoid over-consuming alcohol, caffeine, and sugar. If possible, choose whole foods over packaged items.

Join a support group

A support group for participants struggling with extreme anxiety can provide you with community, structure, encouragement, and advice from others with anxiety disorders. Often led by a counselor, these groups encourage participants to share their struggles and how they have overcome anxiety.

Many support groups engage in activities that bring the group closer. You may role-play or brainstorm solutions to participants’ problems. These sessions are an excellent opportunity to share what has worked for you and to help others.

Consider your inner circle

Toxic friendships and relationships can create extreme anxiety. Consider the relationships you have with those in your inner circle. Is there mutual respect and honor? Is there a form of abuse? If you are in an abusive relationship, seek help immediately.

Remove or limit connections that leave you feeling anxious, drained, or depressed. A counselor can help you shift from these toxic connections to more beneficial ones.

Turn your anxiety over to god

We are hard pressed on every side, but not crushed; perplexed, but not in despair; persecuted, but not abandoned; struck down, but not destroyed. – 2 Corinthians 4:8-9, NIV

The Bible reminds us that we are never alone. The Lord will never leave us. There will always be trouble. Fear and worries may try to overtake us, but God can give peace that no one understands. Jesus reminds us, “Do not let your hearts be troubled. You believe in God; believe also in me.” (John 14:1, NIV)

Don’t give up even when extreme anxiety fills your mind with panic. Pray and ask God to bring you peace and joy like no other. Jesus can handle all of your worries, anxious thoughts, and fears. He can handle all of it. Take it off your shoulders and give it to Him. You can overcome extreme anxiety through Him.

Do you need help with extreme anxiety?

If you have experienced episodes of extreme anxiety or panic attacks, contact our Christian counseling center today to speak to a representative. Our center will connect you to a counselor specializing in anxiety disorders, who can facilitate an assessment and help you create a mental health care plan to overcome extreme anxiety using effective psychological methods and Biblically based principles. Call us today for an appointment.

item.title: Five Things That Negatively Impact Male Mental Health the Most
item.description:
Statistically, men are less often diagnosed with depression than women, and yet are more likely to commit suicide. There is something important about male mental health that lurks in the gap between these two facts: that men are seemingly less depressed than women, but take their own lives in far greater numbers every year.

This disparity raises the question: “Why is it that more men are dealing with depression but not talking about it? Why do more men not seek help when they experience depression?”

Many men suffer silently because they simply don’t have the vocabulary to describe their struggle, while others are just trying to get by without having to ask for help. Men have been raised to believe that asking for help is a sign of weakness, or sold lies about masculinity and mental health. However, the truth of God’s Word will ultimately set men free if they can learn to tune into the right “voices” and obtain correct information.

No man wants to feel impotent or victimized, but the truth is that men do struggle. Being a man does not mean being on par with gods and angels. They bleed, they get hurt, life affects them, and it is only when men acknowledge that they’re stuck or struggling that they can find the help they need to heal or move on.

Maybe it’s time to address the shame and fear that have been holding men back, assess the situation they’re in, and talk to each other about the struggle. In this way, men can begin to make progress as men and as individuals by talking privately and openly with a trusted friend, or even accessing the power of a group of men sharing similar experiences.

You are never truly alone unless you want to be. Jesus Himself was an example of not carrying a burden alone. He shared the challenges he faced with His disciples openly and lovingly, and they responded to Him in kind.

Individuals and the Collective

For the most part, men have been taught that vulnerability is a kind of weakness. To be masculine is to be “strong,” and to be “strong” equates to handling life’s difficulties on their own.

From the youngest age, men are taught that boys don’t cry and that any emotion other than anger and apathy is for the weak. Even the milder depictions of masculinity that were modeled were sometimes toxic, if only because they were built on incomplete understandings of male mental health.

Boys do cry, show hurt, sadness, tenderness, and affection, along with the whole range of human emotions. So do men. Men are mentally, emotionally, and physically complex by design, and that is an important and powerful part of God’s design. Besides this, men are all individuals with unique experiences, insights, skills, and traumas.

Only when people begin to understand and accept men as individuals can we begin to figure out where each of us fits into the collective. There might be some broad cultural ideals that men are expected to meet, but we will each reach these goals by taking our own unique paths to them.

The man who uses his hands to build houses in the village is no less valuable than the man who plants crops and flowers, and no less valuable than the disabled man who is only able to tell stories and speak sense to the next generation.

In the same way, men who show more masculine physical traits and/or limited emotional expression could learn from men around them that there are many benefits to softer, more sensitive emotions, which they often avoid. Each man has different roles, unique struggles, personal pressure points, and each of these things determines value as individuals first and as men second.

At the end of the day, each man is responsible for himself, his spouse or partner, and his family. Some men’s greatest achievement in life is that they are patient and kind toward others, and generous and loving toward themselves as well, even while maintaining ordinary jobs and receiving minimum wage.

Five Things That Negatively Impact Male Mental Health

Regardless of your unique skills, personality, or life experiences, as a man, you will face one or more of the following struggles, statistically speaking. Male mental health is affected by a collection of similar struggles that seem to reach across generations and cultures.

These are the things that we must face head-on, be vocal and honest about as we navigate them, and find our way of getting through them to avoid being part of the tragic statistics. Unfortunately, there is no road map or blueprint for how to get through this stuff. Each man must do his best, help his brothers, accept help from those who love him, and keep going.

Unemployment and Work Struggles

The one aspect of life where men draw our worth from the most is our contribution to society. Men know that if we don’t work, we don’t eat; that’s just how the world works. Sadly, life isn’t just as simple as finding a well-paying job and doing that until retirement.

Sometimes it takes decades to find something that they enjoy doing and are good at, and even then, the job market is so unstable that they aren’t guaranteed employment, a healthy work environment, or a manageable workload.

Few things negatively impact male mental health more than unemployment, especially when it lasts for months and years. Criticism and harsh words around this situation can often cut the deepest in a man’s security in a relationship and his self-image.

At the core, men not only need security and stability, but also to know that they are making a valuable contribution somewhere. They need to know that they are seen and appreciated, even as they struggle. It is not weak or shameful to need to feel valued; in fact, it is a sign that they see their own value.

Money Problems

Men work to contribute something valuable, but also to find financial stability. They might not be able to find a job that offers both, but if they can’t at least find a way to put food on the table and pay bills, their mental health will plummet in a sea of anxiety and fear. When there is the added pressure of having a family to provide for, the strain of not making enough money is enough to sink any man’s health.

Relationship Issues

God said right at the start that it wasn’t good for man to be alone. Many men have learned to cope well with being on their own, but for those with marriages and families, nothing is more tumultuous than a family torn apart by divorce or separation.

Male mental health is often at its lowest when there is a dramatic change in the family and a lack of social support through these changes. Regardless of the cause of these struggles, no man can navigate these experiences alone, and some don’t make it through these struggles alive.

Isolation

Men are more likely to try to cope privately and silently with their problems. Many grew up with fathers who were fixers, who never asked for help and who never modeled vulnerability and humility. Male mental health suffers most in stubborn silence and in isolation.

If you find yourself without a decent support system or without people to talk to or listen to your experiences, make changes as soon as possible. Having even a single confidant or trusted friend can make all the difference to male mental health.

Stigma

Perhaps you are trying to navigate life alone because that’s what was expected of you. That is the case for many men. Here’s the thing about stereotypes and toxic masculinity, though: it kills. If you have spent your entire life internalizing your struggles and externalizing your aggression, you have missed out on some of the most fundamental experiences of being a man.

Brotherhood, vulnerability, accountability, and humility are all vital aspects of masculinity, yet many are bound by misguided, cruel, and damaged depictions of manhood. Lies will keep you bound in fear, but the truth will release you to be the best version of yourself possible.
